Oracle Has Lost Half Its Value. Oppenheimer Still Sees $275 ©@gorodenkoff from Getty Images via Canva, @DKosig from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Oppenheimer kept its Outperform rating and $275 price target on Oracle on Oct. 29, [91%] above the stock's price, after shares lost 49% in a year.

At its Oct. 28 Investor Day, Oracle said free cash flow should turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028. It also said it would raise no more than $20 billion of new financing.

Analysts' earnings estimates have held up, and the stock trades at 17x forward earnings against a five-year average of 21x.

Oppenheimer's target implies 32x forward earnings, a multiple Oracle has rarely reached, so a rebound looks likely to stop well short of $275.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) stock has lost 49% of its value in a year, and Oppenheimer still thinks it's headed to $275.

On Oct. 29, the day after Oracle's Investor Day, analyst Brian Schwartz reiterated his Outperform rating and $275 price target. That's 91% above the stock's $144.34 on Oct. 28.

The AI build got expensive

Oracle spent $55.7 billion on capex in fiscal 2026 (the year to May 2026), against $67.4 billion of revenue, and its free cash flow came to negative $23.7 billion.

Paying for it took outside money. Oracle sold $25 billion of bonds in February. S&P cut its credit rating to BBB-, one step above junk, on July 9. And Oracle finished a $20 billion stock sale in the quarter to Aug. 31.

At its Oct. 28 Investor Day, Oracle said free cash flow should turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and top $30 billion in fiscal 2029. It also said it would raise no more than $20 billion of additional financing.

Oppenheimer hasn't budged

Schwartz raised his target to $275 from $235 in June and named Oracle the firm's top pick for 2026, arguing that its backlog justified the heavier spending.

Can Oracle earn its way to $275?

The consensus target was $236 on Oct. 27, down from $350 a year earlier, and Oppenheimer's $275 is 17% above it.

Oracle (ORCL): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

Earnings estimates haven't come down with it. Analysts expect normalized EPS of $8.14 in fiscal 2027 and $10.99 in fiscal 2028, up from $8.05 and $10.89 three months ago.

Oracle (ORCL): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2028 (years to May) (TIKR)

Investor Day gives them no reason to fall. Oracle reaffirmed its $8.10 forecast for fiscal 2027 and set a target of $21 or more for fiscal 2030.

The stock is cheap against its own history, at 17x forward earnings against a five-year average of 21x.

Oracle Is Up 12% in a Week. Is Its Free Cash Flow Plan Really That Good? ©@yhelfman via Canva, @Yurich84 from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Oracle is up 12% in the past week after its Investor Day dated positive free cash flow and capped new raises at $20 billion.

Its $30 billion free cash flow target for fiscal 2029 is far above the $5.9 billion consensus.

Tuesday's deals bring Alphabet's Google chips, NVIDIA's systems and Cerebras' inference to Oracle's cloud.

OpenAI's share of the backlog is the main risk, but at a below-average P/E, Oracle is a buy for patient investors.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) stock is up 12% in the past week, after its Investor Day finally said when the cash comes back.

Tuesday set it up, with deals to offer Google TPUs from Alphabet (GOOG), NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) superclusters and Cerebras (CBRS:NASDAQ) inference on Oracle's cloud.

Oracle finally put a date on it

On the Sept. 10 call, CFO Hilary Maxson still had no date for positive free cash flow: "We haven't given a particular time frame on that yet."

Oracle had $23.7 billion of negative free cash flow in fiscal 2026 and raised about $50 billion from February to August.

Oracle's Investor Day release changed that:

Positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028 and $30 billion+ in fiscal 2029

New raises through fiscal 2030 capped at $20 billion, half equity and half debt

Net debt, vendor financing included, below 3.5x adjusted EBITDA in fiscal 2029

Consensus has two more years of negative free cash flow, then just $5.9 billion in fiscal 2029:

Oracle (ORCL): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to May) (TIKR)
$20 billion is a lot less than feared

On Tuesday, Evercore estimated Oracle might need another $50 billion to $60 billion for its AI buildout. The cap is less than half that, with vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and prepayments covering the rest.

Wins for Google and Cerebras, a question for NVIDIA

Oracle is the first hyperscaler outside Google to sell Alphabet's TPUs. Cerebras gets a sales channel that doesn't run through OpenAI, which accounts for much of its $25.4 billion of contracted revenue.

Oracle's NVIDIA superclusters are headed to multi-gigawatt scale, but Oracle's capex steps down in fiscal 2029. Do NVIDIA's Oracle sales peak with it?

Is Oracle a buy after the bounce?

Oracle went into Wednesday at 15x forward earnings, far below its 21x five-year average:

Oracle (ORCL): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

Wednesday's jump takes it to about 17x, or about 7x management's $21 fiscal 2030 EPS target.

title: Cerebras Sinks 10% as Short Seller Culper Claims Its Wafers “Break Down After Just ~2 Years”

Cerebras Sinks 10% as Short Seller Culper Claims Its Wafers "Break Down After Just ~2 Years" ©pixelshot and Nikada from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Cerebras Systems fell 10% after short seller Culper Research said its chips wear out in about two years.

The two-year figure is unproven, but Culper's point about Cerebras's own filings needs an answer.

The claim lands on Oracle, which added Cerebras to its cloud on Tuesday alongside NVIDIA and Alphabet chips.

Cerebras Systems (CBRS:NASDAQ) is down 10% today after short seller Culper Research claimed its wafers "break down after just ~2 years in use."

That erases Tuesday's 10% gain on a deal to offer Cerebras systems on the cloud of Oracle (ORCL:NYSE). Oracle also added more chips from NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) and Alphabet (GOOG) that day.

What Culper is claiming

In a thread on X, Culper called it "a lifespan that undermines the entire business."

Culper's next point, from Cerebras's own filings, is more serious. Culper says Cerebras's draft IPO filings through December 2025 gave the systems useful lives of 1.5 to 3 years. Four months later that range was 3 to 5 years, with no explanation. Longer lives mean lower depreciation and fatter margins.

Margins would take the first hit

Cerebras's gross margin rose from 11.7% in fiscal 2022 to 42.3% in fiscal 2024, then slipped to 39.0% in fiscal 2025.

Cerebras Systems (CBRS): gross margin (%), fiscal 2022-2025 (TIKR)

Wafers that wear out sooner would cut into that.

A question for Oracle, and a gift for NVIDIA

Oracle plans to have Cerebras systems in its data centers by the first half of 2027, on top of $28.5 billion of capex in its latest quarter. Who pays if a wafer wears out early? Its Dec. 10 report is the first chance to ask.

NVIDIA gains from any doubt about Cerebras. Oracle said on its first-quarter call that GPU capacity up for renewal was renewed or resold at a 20% premium, mostly on chips four years old or older. NVIDIA's own fast-inference chip, Groq 3 LPX, is in full production. Its Nov. 17 report will show where inference spending is going.

Alphabet's TPUs reach Oracle's cloud in early 2027, a first for a major cloud outside Google. Alphabet reports after today's close, so watch what it says about outside TPU demand.
